The beam is a prismatic, rectangular cross-section member of width b, height h, and span L, made of a homogeneous, isotropic, linear-elastic material with Young's modulus E.
Small-deformation and linear-elastic behavior is assumed throughout.
Euler-Bernoulli beam theory applies: cross-sections that are plane and normal to the longitudinal axis before deformation remain plane and normal after deformation, and transverse shear deformation is neglected.
The neutral axis of the cross-section coincides with the centroidal axis parallel to the width b, located at mid-height.
The beam is subjected to transverse bending loading (distributed and/or point loads) and at least one applied concentrated moment, which together produce a bending moment distribution M(x) along the span.
The second moment of area (area moment of inertia) of the rectangular cross-section about the neutral axis is I = b·h³/12.
The bending normal stress at any fiber located at a signed distance y from the neutral axis, at axial position x, is given by the flexure formula: σ(x, y) = −M(x)·y / I.
The stress distribution across the depth is linear in y, with zero stress at the neutral axis (y = 0) and maximum magnitude at the outermost fibers (y = ±h/2).
The maximum bending stress magnitude at any section is |σ_max| = |M(x)|·(h/2) / I = 6|M(x)| / (b·h²).
The sign convention is: positive M(x) produces compression in fibers with positive y (above the neutral axis) and tension in fibers with negative y, consistent with the right-hand rule for the bending moment vector.
To obtain M(x) explicitly, apply static equilibrium to the beam with the specified transverse loads and applied moments, using the appropriate boundary conditions (e.g., simply supported, cantilever, or fixed-fixed) to resolve reactions, then integrate the shear and moment relations V(x) = dM/dx and q(x) = −dV/dx over the span.
The curvature of the beam is κ(x) = M(x) / (E·I), and the transverse deflection w(x) satisfies E·I·w″(x) = M(x), subject to the governing boundary conditions.
